summary: A caisson light off Gibson Island: its caisson capsized in 1904, was righted, and the light was lit in 1908. Keepers to 1923, a 1964 nuclear test, private owners since 2006.

lens.note: fourth-order lens at commissioning (NRHP); by 1990 a 250 mm acrylic lens replaced a 300 mm acrylic lens (NRHP)

structures.material: brick dwelling and lantern on a cast-iron cylinder and wooden caisson
structures.note: 38-ft octagonal brick dwelling and lantern on a caisson 82 ft below the water (NRHP); a 48-ft square caisson per the Baltimore paper
wooden caisson with a cast-iron cylinder; size disputed (48 ft vs 32 ft square in NRHP footnote)

access.note: Privately owned by BHL, LLC since the 2006 sale. The tower is closed; the nomination says access is by boat; the owners plan prearranged tours. The Coast Guard keeps access for checks on the light.

facts.agency: BHL, LLC (private owners); U.S. Coast Guard retains access for checks on the light

events.note: Lighthouse Board first requests a light for the locality
experimental disk pile fails to plant at the site on 9 September 1898
caisson settles seven feet out of level 21 September; turned flat on its side in a storm 12 October; work halts until spring
caisson righted 30 June 1907 by the bonding company's crews (NRHP)
brick dwelling and lantern built on the caisson
commissioned 1 October 1908 (NRHP, Chesapeake timeline); owners' website gives 10 September 1908 completion
fourth-order Fresnel lens lit at commissioning
assistant keeper Oscar P. Olsen assists a yacht run aground at the mouth of the Magothy River (Bulletin 1916; the yacht's name is garbled in the OCR)
31 July 1921: six men drifting in a yacht all night are helped; Midgett and Linton commended
illuminant changed to acetylene; fog signal discontinued or replaced (see notes); keepers removed
keeper transferred to Point No Point; duties to Sandy Point Shoal keepers
May 1964: SNAP-7B strontium-90 isotopic generator tested (world's first nuclear-powered light, per LighthouseFriends)
windows bricked over; steel door installed against vandals
roof flashing repaired and gallery restored by USCGC Red Birch; 1989-1990 sandblasting (LHF)
listed on the National Register on 2 December 2002
sold at GSA public auction on 28 June 2006 for $260,000 to BHL, LLC

notes_for_editor: Matched by identity: roster.py matched the station by name and position (0.13 km); roster lines are the USLHS archive's own. Spellings: Berentsen (USLHS; the 1915 Bulletin pennant table, Baltimore row, reads 'Berentsen' on the page image, PDF p. 3, printed p. 147; the OCR text reads 'Barentsen', an OCR error), Berensten (LighthouseFriends), Berentson (Chesapeake timeline). Unresolved: (1) Mud depth for the same 1895 borings: the Board's 1895 report says 65 feet; the 1899 report and the NRHP say 55 feet. Both are shown in the story. (2) Caisson size: the NRHP quotes a Baltimore paper for 48 ft square x 23 ft high, its own footnote cites a National Archives plan for 32 ft square; LighthouseFriends quotes the Board's later description as 48 ft at the bottom, 46 on top, 21 ft high. Not reconciled. (3) Congressional approval of the extra $60,000: LighthouseFriends says 1 July 1902; the NRHP gives 28 April 1904 after accepting the design on 10 June 1902. The Chesapeake timeline puts approval in June 1902 and the contract in 1903 at $91,900; the NRHP has the contract in early 1904. (4) Commissioning: NRHP and Chesapeake timeline say 1 October 1908; the owners' website says construction was completed 10 September 1908. (5) The NRHP says the completion came '28 years after it was first requested'; its own dates (1890, 1908) make eighteen years, as LighthouseFriends says. The story says so. (6) The NRHP's righting dates run out of order ('June 30, 1907' righting, 'By November 20, 1906' within 17 degrees). The story quotes both as printed. (7) Fog signal: NRHP says a bell at first, a foghorn 'sometime before 1923', and a fog bell 'Buoy 6C' from 1 May 1923; LighthouseFriends says the 1923 change discontinued the bell; the Chesapeake timeline says a foghorn replaced the bell in 1923. Not reconciled. (8) Nuclear test length: NRHP 'ran for a year'; LighthouseFriends 'removed two years later'; Chesapeake 'just after one year'. Not reconciled. (9) The 1915 Bulletin's fog-hours table is OCR-jumbled for Baltimore; no Baltimore fog figure is used. (10) The 1916 Bulletin rescue: the yacht's name and the exact date are garbled in the OCR; the story gives only the year and the names, which are clean. (11) The Lighthouse Board corpus stops at 1901 for this station; the 1904-1908 build rests on the NRHP, the Evening Star (1904), LighthouseFriends and the Chesapeake timeline, which share some sources (the timeline cites the Board's reports). (12) Newspaper: 'Flaherty caisson' (1902-1908) gave mostly unrelated pages; 'Craighill caisson' (1904-1907) gave four pages, of which only the 31 May 1904 Evening Star was read. (13) The 2006 buyers are private individuals; the story names the company only, not any individual. (14) The owners' website is an interested source and is footnoted as such. (15) The 1921 commendation names are split across OCR columns; the story quotes only the clean fragments ('Thomas P. Midgett, keeper', 'Linton, assistant keeper'). (16) Matched by column position and checked on page images: the 1915 pennant row (PDF p. 3, printed p. 147) and the 1921 commendation (PDF p. 36, printed p. 196: 'Thomas P. Midgett, keeper, and Edward Linton, assistant keeper, Baltimore Light Station, Md.'; the OCR interleaves it with the 'Sunflower' column). The 1916 Olsen sentence is prose OCR text (PDF p. 31) and was not checked on the image. (17) The NRHP's 1923 fog-signal entry (a fog bell, Buoy 6C, from 1 May 1923) is reported beside the Chesapeake and LighthouseFriends versions. (18) The Chesapeake timeline's June 1902 approval is added beside LighthouseFriends' 1 July 1902 and the nomination's 28 April 1904.
